### Countermodels of the pair of versions: five false proofs of agreement, reproduced and handed to the preservation stream

[`ada891f44fd6`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/ada891f44fd6275e600916e1bf5f009ea5a3f2e4) · [log `5fdbc05d089c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/5fdbc05d089c8341bdc0b2c1e0ddfd20fe18222609a7f6f3a52da36f83c56979.jsonl.gz)

The challenge stream's item 1. lib/tests/fixtures/pairing-countermodels holds two versions of five methods that differ when each runs alone on a JVM and that RegressionPair.agree (lib/src/pairing.rs) proves agreeing: the previous version sets the default locale the new one lowers under; a library static shared without --before-classpath; two unrelated RuntimeExceptions, and IllegalArgumentException against a subclass, compared by category; a scope that is false everywhere but sets the default locale before both calls. All five were Verified on the checker at lupovnmv. The order of the calls is observable: with the versions' roles swapped, and with --before-classpath, the shared-static case is a violation.

### Countermodels of observed class initializers and of class files the tool read where a JVM reads another: three handed to the evidence stream, two refused

[`ec10de45d5a0`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/ec10de45d5a0eebb717cc78a9d412c14a313427b) · [log `5fdbc05d089c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/5fdbc05d089c8341bdc0b2c1e0ddfd20fe18222609a7f6f3a52da36f83c56979.jsonl.gz)

Challenge stream, item 2. lib/tests/fixtures/observed-countermodels holds five fixtures, and lib/tests/observed_countermodels.rs holds each to what a JVM prints. Each was a false proof on the checker as it was (yypzyxmw): crossed, the outside review's A.&lt;clinit> { B.x = 1; k = 7; } (result == 0 proved, a JVM gives 1); lowered, "I".toLowerCase() observed in a Turkish JVM (result == 305 proved, and the locale assumption gone from the result); configured, System.getProperty observed with the property set; released, a class of a multi-release JAR (the tool read the base file where a JVM 17+ loads META-INF/versions/17, so result == 1 was proved where a JVM gives 20, and an observation of the versioned class was put on the base file's code); shadowed, a class path copy of the JDK's org.xml.sax.helpers.AttributesImpl (result == 42 proved, a JVM gives 0).

The first three are the evidence stream's to fix (its brief's item 5 binds an observation): the checker-side test is in the fixtures' README and is sent to its inbox as a failure item. The last two are holes in the class path reader, which no stream owns, so they are refused here: ClassPath::refused (lib/src/classpath.rs) refuses by name, on load and when a class is copied for a pair, a class a multi-release JAR holds a versioned file of, and a class an entry holds in a package of the JDK's image, unless its file is the image's own byte for byte or one of the tool's models (the tool puts both on class paths itself; a first, broader version failed 13 tests for that reason). Enumerating every class still reads the first file, so that walks over which classes exist see it. Not covered: an override only a versioned file declares, and resources.

### Models on request of ArrayDeque and HashSet take example 286's DataBinder.bind past its binding result, to the reflection

[`f3dd56af1d8f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/f3dd56af1d8f26d8ea8383118af084928bf1c1bf) · [log `f9a03c590446`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f9a03c59044607197c9620b9f0316285b55d44dc196fc1b084e03c63fa0eae4f.jsonl.gz)

Every path of DataBinder.bind makes a binding result whose AbstractErrors keeps an ArrayDeque of nested paths and whose AbstractBindingResult a HashSet of suppressed fields; both constructors were JDK gaps under strict gaps. Two models on request now stand for them, as ArrayList's does (lib/models/java/util/lists, models::ON_REQUEST): ArrayDeque as a stack (ArrayDeque(), push with its NullPointerException for null, pop with its NoSuchElementException, peek, size, isEmpty, clear) and HashSet as the keys of the HashMap model (HashSet(), add, contains, size, isEmpty). Both are abstract, as the HashMap model is, so every method they do not keep stays the JDK call it names. AbstractSet() is now an exact JDK call (gaps::exact_jdk_call), as AbstractCollection() and AbstractList() were. Documented in lib/models/README.md and lib/README.md.

Evidence: claims.Deques and claims.Sets (lib/tests/claims.rs, two tool-tier tests) prove each method's JDK answer against its definition written out on every input of a bound with the model, show the class is the JDK's gap when the check does not ask for it and that a method left out (offer, remove) is still the JDK call, and run the same methods on a JVM over 5000 sampled inputs. A mutated model (pop returning the first element; add always true) fails each test. test_costs.py run --changed passed (33 test binaries), validate_example.py 286 passed, examples/tools/test_beside_route.py passed.

Example 286's driver: this line was rebased onto the evidence stream's rkxyyqwn (inbox domain-advances-state-I002), whose shared module examples/tools/beside_route.py now does the three properties; the conflict in proofs/prove.py was resolved into tvxyzwqv by taking the shared module's driver and keeping only each claim's own arguments (ENTRIES: entry, models, observed initializers, unwinding). The decision claim's runs are unchanged from the evidence stream's (no model, the verifier's default unwinding); the protected-state claim's take the three models, unwind 16 and --observed-initializer for PropertyEditorRegistrySupport and CachedIntrospectionResults. Probes at bound 2 (trials, capped at 5 min and 4 GB) of vulnerable-protected-state-mutation now stop at CachedIntrospectionResults.strongClassCache, a ConcurrentHashMap the observation does not hold: the reflection. Inbox item domain-advances-evidence-I006 asks the evidence stream to coordinate observed.rs's format before step 3 extends it. Nothing decided; the frozen claim and the accepted statement are unchanged. The queued job 20261117-130335-example-286-protected-state-tasks-at-the runs the driver as it is now.

### A write set, a first effect contract: prove --writes refutes the setter that writes a protected field and proves its honest twin

[`dfb25346d236`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/dfb25346d2367b9ce36946b5ca6fba175f5e0cf0) · [log `f9a03c590446`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f9a03c59044607197c9620b9f0316285b55d44dc196fc1b084e03c63fa0eae4f.jsonl.gz)

The state stream's steps 4 and 5, the checking side. prove --writes this.displayName (own checker only) states which fields of a method's receiver and object parameters it may write. The check proves the frame with the property: after a normal return every other field of those inputs is unchanged, a primitive by value and a String or object by identity through the new p == \old(p) term. The frame is conjoined to the assertion, so a write outside the set is refuted by the harness and its witness runs on a JVM. Inside the call the engine refuses, by name, a write to anything else that existed before it: a static field, an array, an object no input is (even one a named field holds), or a class initialization, whose objects would look new to the call. This generalizes Engine::keeps through bmc::Options::frame. The cache refuses such a check, since its key does not read the write set.

### An effect contract at a call: a setter's checked write set stands in for its calls, and the application-level rename statement is proved through the honest setter and refuted through the adversarial one

[`085d15514aad`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/085d15514aadb09b9e5ab9b46074f9d77d0dbbe9) · [log `f9a03c590446`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f9a03c59044607197c9620b9f0316285b55d44dc196fc1b084e03c63fa0eae4f.jsonl.gz)

A lemma with a writes: line is now an effect contract of a public instance method (prove --lemmas). It is proved first with its frame (the write set of the last commit) and also as reading nothing that was there before the call: no field of the receiver or an object argument, no static field that is not final, no array, no default locale, and no identity comparison of such an object (bmc::Options::closed_frame, which generalizes Engine::reads and Engine::compares as the write set generalized Engine::keeps). What the method writes is then a function of its arguments. In the check, a call on a receiver of exactly the contract's class, with arguments within its bounds, runs a stub of the claim's class (bmc::Effect, the effect intrinsic). A written field takes the parameter the assertion gives it (this.f == p; the expression language now compares a String field with a String parameter by identity), another written primitive takes any value, and nothing else changes. Elsewhere the method runs as written. A written reference field with no parameter, assume:, throws:, array parameters and non-integral results are refused by name.

Verified with lib/tests/fixtures/claims Frames: the honest setter's contract is proved and used (the statement lists it among what the run rests on), and 'an admin stays one under the new name' is proved. The adversarial setter's contract is refuted, so the check that rests on it is refused. Without it, 'a rename makes no account an admin' is refuted by a rename to admin:, and the witness replays. Five use-side countermodels each grant admin on a JVM (Frames.main): a name past the contract's bound, a receiver field a caller set, a static switch, a literal's identity, a subclass hook called through the inherited setter. Each was a false proof with its rule switched off (by mutation: closed_frame off, the exact-class check off, the stub's bounds guard off). New tests: two tool tests in claims.rs and unit tests for the stub, the conjunct split and String identity; test_costs run --changed passes and lint agrees. Inbox item domain-advances-state-I003 is taken in Progress. The brief is not wrong.

### A library method the own checker can't run may be replaced by a stand-in sampled against it on a JVM (prove --stand-in), and a result that used one says it rests on it

[`cc50b5aaf171`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/cc50b5aaf1713192a9250970a51a8cd821d20901) · [log `f9a03c590446`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f9a03c59044607197c9620b9f0316285b55d44dc196fc1b084e03c63fa0eae4f.jsonl.gz)

Step 3, option 2, of the state stream's brief. Spring's bean wrapper resolves a property through its introspection caches and java.beans and calls the setter with Method.invoke, on every path of DataBinder.bind (example 286). Observing those caches is refused, and running them would need models of java.beans and java.lang.reflect. So the binding path gets a stand-in instead. Each public static method of the stand-in class (but main) replaces an instance method: its first parameter's class is the exact class of the receivers it covers, the rest of its descriptor is the method's. A call resolving to that method on a receiver of exactly that class runs the stand-in. A subclass's receiver, and the stand-in's own calls, run the method as written, so a stand-in hands back what it does not cover. Its main prints one line per sample with the method's outcome and the stand-in's. The tool runs it first on the check's class path and takes the stand-in only if every sample is the same, refusing it by the first input that differs, or when nothing is sampled, or for a public method that replaces nothing. A result that used a stand-in names it among what it rests on, with the number of samples, as sampled evidence and not a proof. A refutation through one is still replayed on a JVM. JBMC and --cache are refused.

Verified by lib/tests/stand_in.rs on the fixture lib/tests/fixtures/stand-ins, a reflective property writer. With the stand-in, a claim the method leaves undecided is proved and the stand-in is named; a refutation replays on a JVM. ### A preservation proof is non-vacuous only with a witness outside the allowed change, and accept.py asks the outcome to say so

[`677bfee17743`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/677bfee17743c0ce042029b3e8f788bbc1ebcc84) · [log `5fdbc05d089c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/5fdbc05d089c8341bdc0b2c1e0ddfd20fe18222609a7f6f3a52da36f83c56979.jsonl.gz)

Step 4 of the evidence stream's brief. A regression check made as a property of the pair of versions (lib/src/pairing.rs, the route of examples 289's and 290's preservation) proves RegressionPair.agree, which returns true on an input inside the allowed change without calling either version. The property check's vacuity probe asked only for an input of the assumption, so it called a proof non-vacuous even when every assumed input lay inside the change. The control: example 289's preservation through its own driver, with only --unchanged-unless replaced by true, was verified and non-vacuous (a capped 5 s probe). 290's recorded witness, servlets=[], lies inside its own allowed change.

The fix: a verified pair with an allowed change is checked once more, meantToChange against result over the same assumption, domain and class path. A proof makes the statement vacuous; a witness, replayed as any is, becomes the statement's, with the new stated.vacuity.outside naming the change. The regression harness's own probe sets outside too, since that harness returns before the probe on an input in the scope. Now the true control is vacuous, 289 with its own change is non-vacuous at servletPath="" (0.3 s more) and 290 at servlets=[0] (capped probes, recorded in both examples' notes). accept.py refuses an establishment of a task with an allowed change whose outcome does not say its witness lies outside that change (unbound) or names another (fail). So 289's and 290's accepted preservation answers are refused until a rerun on a checker with this fix; the other six stay accepted.

Verified: lib/tests/pairing.rs a_pairs_proof_is_vacuous_when_the_allowed_change_covers_every_assumed_input (tool tier, fails without the fix with NonVacuous), three new cases in examples/tools/test_accept.py, the 289 checkout test now expecting preservation refused for this reason; test_costs.py run --changed 8 of 8, estimate, tag and lint clean; validate_example.py 289 and 290 pass. lib/README.md describes the check.

The brief's 'Where it stands' paragraph is out of date: 289's and 290's preservation are refused now, and every accepted answer of 289 and 290 carries no limit about unrecorded artifacts.

### Countermodels of a checked summary: seven false proofs past the foundation's refusals, refused

[`569cf0dada85`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/569cf0dada85b815e844bb026f031471163b717f) · [log `01f31b73ec60`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/01f31b73ec60a898d86cb426a7758c10ef50f886c8e8dc39edf35ae8372ca59c.jsonl.gz)

Item 3 of the challenge brief. Seven lemmas were proved and their summaries made the checker prove properties a JVM contradicts (fixtures in lib/tests/fixtures/lemma-countermodels, its README has the table).

The first group is an initializer cycle that calls the lemma's method before the final static field it reads is written (seen and heldSeen: proved 7, a JVM gives 0). The foundation's guard looked only at the method's own class.

The second is a final static whose initializer, run by the lemma's proof in the harness's state, reads what a caller changes before it initializes the class: a static (setThenOwn), the default locale (turkishThenLowered) and another class's array (setThenCopied).

The third is a StringBuilder a final static holds, read by the model directly or through a method reference (appendThenLogged and appendThenLoggedThroughLambda). The model's reads never asked Engine::reads.

Summaries are no stream's this run, so they are refused here (lib/src/bmc/mod.rs, strings.rs). No summary is used while any class is being initialized; the call runs as written, so seen and heldSeen are now violations, as on a JVM. Class initializers a lemma's proof runs are held to the lemma's read gate, and objects there when one starts or returns count as there before the call. A lemma reads no StringBuilder that was there before the call.

### The checker models a line logged at WARNING as spring-jcl logs it, so example 287's preservation reaches both sides' bcrypt

[`99156cb31cf5`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/99156cb31cf54c64fd5905966dfec3e674068142) · [log `9090e861ccdd`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/9090e861ccddf9e655c71c2377a905c5373576a92bb47804927954df873d7873.jsonl.gz)

java.util.logging at INFO, WARNING and SEVERE is now modelled under the JDK's default configuration (lib/src/bmc/runtime.rs). isLoggable is true there. A LogRecord's constructor of a level and a message (NullPointerException for a null level) and its setters do nothing a check observes. A Logger's resource bundle and bundle name are null. Logger.log(record) returns normally under a second stated assumption: the record goes only to the root's default ConsoleHandler, and no logger has a filter, handler or bundle. The handler formats the record by calling its getters, which a subclass may override. So log is modelled only for a record whose class below LogRecord writes nothing but its own fields and calls nothing but its own methods, LogRecord's, String's, StackTraceElement's and a Throwable's constructors and getters. A bytecode scan checks this, and spring-jcl's LocationResolvingLogRecord passes. A logging call the model does not take is now the gap it is to a checker without the model; before, an isLoggable the model declined was counted exact. String.valueOf(Object) of a String or null is modelled before the static classification, so the gap scan still names it for other objects.

Countermodels came first, in lib/tests/fixtures/claims/claims/Logged.java. On a JVM each returns false or throws where a model that took logging for granted would say true: a record that counts its formatting, a level, a filter and a handler set on a logger, and valueOf of an object whose toString counts. All five now stop the proof. With the confinement scan disabled, the counting record was falsely verified. The claims test a_line_logged_at_warning_returns_normally_and_what_would_make_logging_observable_stops_the_proof also proves the warned path, the null cases and loud. P.loud moved there, since INFO is now modelled. lib/README.md and 287's notes say what changed.

Probes on example 287's preservation: a trial at bound 8 verifies. At the claim's bound of 80, with a 200 s timeout, the pair reaches both sides' bcrypt and ends on a spurious counterexample past the invariants of BCrypt.crypt_raw and ekskey; a JVM run shows it is no counterexample. This is the relational failure the stream's brief predicts, and step 2 starts from it. Verified with test_costs.py run --changed (26 of 26), the lint, and validate_example.py 287.

### /single-agent-run: one agent toward one outcome, with a watcher that judges after each cycle and can change what the next one is told

[`5bb59759e1d9`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/5bb59759e1d9887f19274e921459bbef18a8f417) · [log `f05af75c6619`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f05af75c6619512ffa6ff1491e42f4d082eb7528774c3f2817f0c5ea1decc23a.jsonl.gz)

A third kind of watched run, beside /prove-java-change and /run-brief, for a goal well within one agent's reach, where a brief with streams is more than the work needs. The command takes a starting prompt, an optional brief file and a continue message. The first cycle is given the prompt, and every later one the run's continue message as it stands when that cycle starts, so the user can have the watcher change it between two cycles and steer a run that is under way. Both texts reach the agent word for word; a brief adds one sentence after each that names the file. After every cycle (one context window: the loop compacts the session after each) the watcher is given the agent's report, the cycle's commits, what it left uncommitted and the queue, and answers continue or stop; each answer is a decision in llm-dlc/decisions/single-NAME.jsonl.

The loop is a new mode of feature-loop.sh, single-agent, so a run has what every loop has: the memory cap, the record the loop statistics read, the session's own compaction at 600k tokens put to the watcher when no commit came, the closing summary, a count of cycles that can be changed while it runs. It differs from the other loops in one rule: a cycle with no commit does not stop it, because the watcher reads what that means (the outcome reached, a question, or stuck). Without a verdict in time (15 minutes, --verdict-wait) a cycle that committed is followed by another, one that did not ends the run before its compact as in every loop, and three in a row without a verdict end it, since nothing else measures such a run. llm-dlc/tools/single_run.py is the watcher's tool: start (in the checkout or in a jj workspace of its own, a new session, a continued one or a fork), wait, answer, message, status, summary, cycles, stop, jobs (for a run stopped only to wait on verification jobs), collect and land. It keeps the verification queue as a brief's watcher does, through brief_run.py's own functions, unless another run's watcher keeps it. The skill is .claude/skills/single-agent-run; llm-dlc/README.md has a section on it.

Also fixed in feature-loop.sh, for every loop: a stop that reached the loop before a cycle began (typed, or left by a watcher, before the first cycle or between the last look and the next cycle) was counted as a cycle to start, which left the count below zero, and nothing ended the loop. It now ends there. loop_stats.py reads the new record (every text such a run sent is a cycle, a cycle with no commit does not take the decision after it for the last commit's, and the watcher's own words for an ending are not matched against the other endings).

Verified with llm-dlc/tools/test_single_run.py (13 tests: the loop run for real in a made-up jj repository with a stand-in claude, through each of the above, a workspace made and landed, a fork, a stop and a restart included), and test_costs.py run --changed: 16 of 16 files passed, test_prove_loop.py (30) and test_brief_run.py (39) among them. No real session was started: the first run is the user's.

### A single-agent run's continue message is a person's alone: the watcher can no longer set it

[`4b5cb3634b87`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4b5cb3634b87a6c9cb6b78be2475ae62072c3b6f) · [log `f05af75c6619`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f05af75c6619512ffa6ff1491e42f4d082eb7528774c3f2817f0c5ea1decc23a.jsonl.gz)

The user's decision on 2026-11-18, after reading the first version: the continue message is an option for a person to steer the session, given with an expert's review and written to account for a long run, and the watcher is never to modify it; the loop ending is preferred to a watcher steering, in almost all cases. The first version let the watcher set the message when the user asked, with an answer or by the message command.

Now single_run.py message sets the message only for a person at their own terminal (stdin and stdout a terminal and no CLAUDECODE in the environment, the test sync.py uses for its approvals) and is refused from a session with words that say what to do instead: end the run and say why. The answer command takes no message any more, and start refuses --continue on a run that already exists, so a restart cannot change it either. Printing the message and its history stays open to all. The question a watcher is given after a cycle says the message is never its to change and that stop is the answer when the run should not go on as it reads. The skill tells the watcher not to set it, edit its file, draft a replacement unasked, or get a new text to the agent another way, and to answer stop when the next cycle would need to be told something the message does not say; if the user asks it for a change, it gives them the command to run themselves. The README section says the same.

Verified with test_single_run.py (13 tests; the changed one shows the refusal from a session, a person's change taken by the next cycle and recorded as theirs, an answer that carries no message, and a restart that cannot change it) and test_costs.py run --changed: 16 of 16 files passed. In an earlier of the two runs of that command test_prove_loop.py failed once and passed when run again, with the machine at a load of 23 to 29 from the brief run under way; alone it passed three times in a row, and its tests wait one second for a verdict, which a loaded machine can miss. Which test it was is not known: the first run's output was not kept.

### A brief's watcher gets a merge order and early merges, a stream's rerun, helpers, and a default test run only when it is due

[`a10468dae7dc`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/a10468dae7dc35f2bcb256a56fe88a4384762ade) · [log `f05af75c6619`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f05af75c6619512ffa6ff1491e42f4d082eb7528774c3f2817f0c5ea1decc23a.jsonl.gz)

What the domain-advances run (2026-11-17) showed the /run-brief watcher could not do, from an agent's analysis of that run and the user's notes on it. Seven of its ten points are built here; three are left out at the user's word (help deciding when to stop, the stale cost in summaries, and cleaning up workspaces at the end, which could lose data).

Merges that interact. `brief_run.py trial BRIEF` merges every pair of the streams' lines, and each with the default line, beside every working copy (`jj new --no-edit`, read, abandoned) and lists the files each pair conflicts in beyond the generated ones and the test inventory. `brief_run.py order BRIEF STREAM ...` records a merge order: `merge` refuses a stream while one before it has commits the line lacks, and the held-back stream's merge question names what to merge first. `merge BRIEF STREAM --early` merges a stream that is still at work as far as it has committed, leaving its uncommitted files, its question and the brief's status alone. In that run two streams conflicted in one file and the stream held back was answered `leave` for four hours.

A stream whose loop died (VF-037). `brief_run.py rerun BRIEF STREAM` leaves a request that run-streams.sh takes once the stream's own process has ended: the loop starts again inside the run, with its counts at nought, and is put to the watcher to merge when finished; after the run has ended the same command starts it again for that stream. Before any loop starts, run-streams.sh stops a scope that holds only what an ended loop left (the tests a session killed for memory was running), which is what made the restart fail and count as the stream's second failure; a scope with a loop at work in it is left alone.

Helpers. The user names a Claude Code session they have open, by its tmux pane (`/run-brief --helper "tmux 3"`, or later in words); the first is for low-hanging work and others may be added with a role of their own. `brief_run.py helper BRIEF add|task|done|merge|list`: a task is the watcher's text wrapped in a stream's standing rules, the helper's workspace is put at the default line's one last commit (never from a merge in progress), one line naming the task's file is typed into the pane (never into a pane at a shell prompt), the helper reports with `done`, `wait` returns it, and the watcher merges it. The skill also says how material from outside the run comes in (new files only, merged by the watcher, acknowledged through an inbox item of the new kind `delivered`) and when to suggest a specialist (the same wall for two cycles).

Who commits what. `wait` now commits the run's decision record whenever it has changed, the user's answers with the watcher's, under a message that says so (a user's answer had gone into a commit of results under that commit's message); the skill says to record an action only after it happened. feature-loop.sh drops its own and the run's variables before it starts `claude`, so a stream's test of these scripts can no longer put made-up questions to the real watcher, and the preflight refuses a watcher whose own environment carries a run's variables.

Tests. A change to lib/tests/costs.json no longer chooses any test in `test_costs.py run --changed` (it ran all of cargo test, which filled a stream's memory in VF-037), and a change to test_costs.py or cost_tier.py chooses the one Rust binary that reads them, `tiers`, not all of them. `default_run.py after-merge` runs the default test run after a merge only when the last one in the checkout failed or none passed there within the hour, and with `--final` whenever no passed run covers the commit, in a memory cap of its own (8G) with two Rust test binaries at a time. CLAUDE.md's Tests section, lib/README.md and both watcher skills say to use it after a merge: the user asked for the default run to be run less, and never because of the inventory.

Verified by 16 new tests (trial merges, the order, early merges, reruns inside and after a run, the scope cleared, helpers, the environment check, the due check) and: the tests of what changed passed, 25 of 25 (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap: the tiers binary of cargo test and 24 Python test files, among them all 50 tests of test_brief_run.py and the 13 of test_single_run.py), and the inventory's lint agrees. No real run has used any of this yet; the first /run-brief after the merge is the first end-to-end check. Nothing here is merged into the default line, where the domain-advances run's watcher is still at work.

### A loop's session can be carried by Codex: one client boundary, models resolved at launch, the same instructions and skills for both clients

[`f5cb8beb2977`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/f5cb8beb29775f32e6201363e390431cb3e2871b) · [log `f05af75c6619`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f05af75c6619512ffa6ff1491e42f4d082eb7528774c3f2817f0c5ea1decc23a.jsonl.gz)

Brief 00 ("Run Codex and Claude Code from the same loop instructions", the user's, 2026-11-18): give the operator a choice of Codex or Claude Code for a loop's worker, with the briefs, the instruction of a cycle, the commit check, the conductor, the queue and the record unchanged. This is the worker's side of it, built on the current loops and not on the 2026-11-16 proof of concept's copies, whose findings it reuses.

The boundary is one file, llm-dlc/tools/agent_client.py. It starts a Codex turn (`codex exec --json`), resumes the session's own thread (`codex exec resume THREAD`), and prints the stream the loops already read from Claude Code (init, assistant text and tool calls, compact_boundary, one closing result), so the progress display, the compaction watch, a cycle's report and the cost accounting keep their one reader; Claude Code's turns are started as before, argument for argument. A loop names its session by a UUID and Codex names its thread itself: the binding is written whole when Codex reports the thread, a later turn resumes exactly that thread, and a client that reports another ends the turn as an error. Each attempt keeps Codex's events, its stderr, its last message and a digest of what it was given. Compaction between cycles is asked of Codex's app server (`thread/compact/start`), because `/compact` sent as a turn is only text. A failed turn, a stream that ends with no result, a cancelled turn and a mismatched thread each end as a result the loop can read.

Models are resolved once: a brief keeps its model's name, and the operator's equivalences give Astra 6.2 for Fable 5.2 and Sol 6.2 for Opus 5.5; a model with no equivalent is refused before a turn is spent, and the effort is always passed on (the machine's own Codex default is another). The client is chosen at the start and kept: `single_run.py start --client codex`, `brief_run.py start --agent codex` or `--stream-agent b=codex` for a mixed run, `brief_run.py foundation --agent codex`, a brief's `- client:` setting, FEATURE_LOOP_CLIENT. The preflight shows each stream's client, model and effort, and blocks an unmapped model, a Codex stream that would fork a Claude Code conversation, and a Codex that is not given this checkout's CLAUDE.md.

What was tried live on Codex CLI 0.169 before building, on scratch threads: the event format; resume by thread id; compaction through the app server, after which the thread still knew what it had read; and approvals. A headless turn with approval_policy on-request alone cannot ask to leave the sandbox, and added writable folders do not open the repository's store, so a worker in a sibling jj workspace could not commit; `--approve-for-me` (the workspace-write sandbox, requests reviewed automatically) let it, and is what a turn is started with, as the counterpart of the `--permission-mode auto` the loops give Claude Code.

One source for each instruction. Codex reads this repository's CLAUDE.md in place (project_doc_fallback_filenames, on the command line because a fresh sibling workspace is not a trusted project, and in .codex/config.toml). The skills are the files under .claude/skills, reached through relative links in .agents/skills; publish and review-findings, which only the user may start, say so for Codex too (agents/openai.yaml). `agent_client.py instructions --client codex` renders what the model would be given without calling one and checks it (CLAUDE.md's first and last lines present, nothing shadowing it, within the byte budget, each skill linked, no user-only skill offered to a work turn), printing paths, digests and pass or fail; run against the real client here it passes, and the two user-only skills are absent from the list Codex is offered. The three watcher skills now name both models approved for the watcher's role, Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.2, where they told any other model to stop.

Identity, authority and cost. A Codex started from a Claude Code session would inherit that session's identity: the boundary removes it and keeps who started the loop in the binding, and a job is submitted under Codex's own thread. The person-only guards (sync.py allow approve, review accept, the single-agent run's continue message, prune_workspaces) now recognize Codex's mark on the commands it runs as they did Claude Code's, since Codex may give a command a terminal. Codex reports tokens and no dollars, so a Codex turn's cost is unknown and is shown so ($? or $1.50+?, with its tokens) in the progress line, the status bar and the summaries, never as nought.

Not in this commit: Codex sessions in the published traces (sync.py does not read Codex's logs, and must not before the redaction rules cover Codex's account identifiers; the proof of concept's reader and policy 5 are to be ported and the rules stamped), Codex hooks, the proof stages of /prove-java-change, and runtime checkouts. llm-dlc/loops/codex-pilot.md is the small two-stream brief the live rehearsals use.

Verified by 29 new tests over a stand-in for the client (llm-dlc/tools/codex_standin.py): the adapter's 19, a two-cycle single-agent run carried by the stand-in through the real feature-loop.sh (the user's prompt and continue message reach it word for word, the thread is compacted by the client between the cycles and resumed, nothing of the run or of the watcher's identity reaches the worker, and Claude Code runs no turn), a run's choice of client per stream, and unknown costs. The tests of what changed passed, 31 of 31 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap; no Rust input changed), and the files edited after that run started were run again (test_single_run, test_prove_loop, test_agent_client, test_runs, test_loop_stats, test_inbox: all pass). The live two-cycle rehearsals with real Codex workers follow this commit, from workspaces made from it.

### Every Codex turn is given its sandbox and approvals, a resumed one too; and a session asks a Codex thread by a tool, not by typing into its terminal

[`170f53f47f35`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/170f53f47f35806197cb88c517fde35035697156) · [log `f05af75c6619`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f05af75c6619512ffa6ff1491e42f4d082eb7528774c3f2817f0c5ea1decc23a.jsonl.gz)

The first live rehearsal of a Codex worker (a Sol 6.2 session on llm-dlc/loops/codex-pilot-a.md through feature-loop.sh, in the disposable workspace codex-pilot-a) found what the stand-in could not: its first cycle wrote its note, committed it with sync.py commit and was compacted through the app server, and its second cycle, a resumed turn, found the workspace read-only with approvals off, changed nothing and said so, so the loop stopped with 'no commit, session needs attention'. Codex's own log shows why: 'codex exec resume' takes no sandbox flag and does not keep the thread's, so a resumed turn falls back to exec's read-only default. agent_client.py now gives every turn, new or resumed, the three settings that --approve-for-me stands for (sandbox_mode workspace-write, approval_policy on-request, approvals_reviewer auto_review); a probe on a scratch repository confirmed that a resumed turn given them writes a file and commits with jj from a sibling workspace.

llm-dlc/tools/ask_codex.py is how a Claude Code session asks a Codex thread a question, after this session's attempt to type one into the expert's tmux window was refused by the permission check, and rightly: a pasted text races the person at that terminal and the answer has to be read off a screen. 'ask --thread NAME --prompt-file FILE' runs one read-only turn of a thread of its own (the first question to a name forks an existing session, which is left as it was, or starts an empty one; later questions resume it) and returns the answer as data with a timeout; the outgoing text goes through the project's redaction rules first and a finding refuses it, since a question leaves the machine; every exchange is kept as a file under llm-dlc/loop-summaries/exchanges. 'mail send|list|read' is a file mailbox for the way back, which a Codex session can write with a shell command, and 'note' leaves a line in a session a person has open (codex queue). An answer or a message is advice for the receiving session to judge, never an instruction or a person's approval, and each says so. The design is the one recommended to this session by the user's session in tmux 4; the permission rule it suggests for the tool is the user's to add, and this commit adds none.

Verified by 7 new tests over the stand-in client (a first question, a fork and a resumed question, a timeout that stops the client, a failed turn, a refused text of which nothing is sent or kept, a queued note, a message's life in a mailbox) and the changed adapter tests, which now require the same three settings on a resumed turn as on the first; the tests of what changed pass, 4 of 4 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap). The live rehearsal is run again from this commit.

[`068f7e3a8d81`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/068f7e3a8d8141f9ae64cdf0fe2a16bfad5cce06) · [log `f05af75c6619`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f05af75c6619512ffa6ff1491e42f4d082eb7528774c3f2817f0c5ea1decc23a.jsonl.gz)

Codex traces a session under its own thread id, not the id the loop gave it, so feature-loop.sh now writes 'Codex thread THREAD carries session SESSION.' into its record once the thread exists (in the header for a session that is continued, after the first turn for a new one; 'agent_client.py thread' prints it), and loop_stats.py, sync.py's publishing of run records and tool_time.py's discovery take the thread for the session where the record has that line.

Codex's model calls a tool that runs commands, and the log has the call and each command: tool_time.py takes the commands for the calls where a batch has them, so a wait is counted once and filed by what ran. Checked on the real log and records of the Astra rehearsal before its workspace was removed: two runs found by their records (2 cycles with 2 commits, then 1 cycle with none), 418 s of the first prompt's 418 s accounted for (404 s the model, 20 s tools; it was 4 s of model time before), the commit's 19 s filed under sync.py, every cost shown as '?'. ### Codex sessions get the checkout's two hooks: the adapter runs them after each turn it carried, and .codex/hooks.json names them for a trusted checkout

[`4c94f7daf581`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4c94f7daf5816dd0d9568a1b5e1495c503d975c1) · [log `f05af75c6619`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/f05af75c6619512ffa6ff1491e42f4d082eb7528774c3f2817f0c5ea1decc23a.jsonl.gz)

Brief 00. Claude Code runs two hook commands from .claude/settings.json: 'sync.py hook' at a turn's end (finished turns to Langfuse, where that is set up) and 'sync.py hook-commit' after a shell command (a commit made without sync.py gets its session's trace). A Codex session had neither. Both commands now take Codex's payload, whose transcript_path is the session's rollout: the session id is read from the rollout's name, and a Codex log is sent to Langfuse read whole, each prompt remembered by an id made of its turn and line (codex_rollout.claude_view gives prompts that id), so no turn is sent twice.

Where they run from was the question. Codex loads a project's hooks only from a project a person trusted, and runs only hooks a person reviewed; a loop's worker runs in a fresh sibling workspace, which is neither. Probes from a scratch folder (Codex CLI 0.169) showed: hooks given with -c run only with --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust; a project's .codex/hooks.json did not run even with that flag and a trust_level given with -c ('Untrusted project-local configuration is disabled'); a hook's command goes through a shell. The bypass flag would also run every other unreviewed hook, so agent_client.py runs the two commands itself after each Codex turn, with the payload Codex's hooks get: hook-commit when a command of the turn made a plain commit, then hook. A failure is written beside the attempt (*.hooks.log) and stops nothing; AGENT_CLIENT_HOOKS=off turns it off. .codex/hooks.json names the same two commands for a session a person runs in a trusted checkout; that Codex loads that file was not verified, since it needs a person's review in /hooks (the same definitions ran when given inline, and both commands pass a pipe-test with status 0 and no output).

Verified by a real Codex turn through agent_client.py in a scratch jj repository with a recording stand-in for sync.py: both commands ran, given the real rollout named by the thread; by four new tests (the Stop payload and the commit hook through the stand-in, a hook that fails, the two hook files naming the same commands, a Codex log sent turn by turn by hook_export); and by the tests of what changed, 21 of 21 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap).

### A Codex turn's own compactions reach the loop, and a decision in the allow list that no person took is an error of check

[`9fbf550ad9d3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9fbf550ad9d3f3bff92223ebee894f7ba412727a) · [log `7e2551ec657f`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/7e2551ec657f3acbdd40271e6c6496783fe074a6f5877cb9fb7138ee8c9b2e92.jsonl.gz)

Two things brief 00 had left open, taken up at the user's word and settled by probes of Codex CLI 0.169 from scratch folders (2026-11-19).

Automatic compaction in the middle of a turn: 'codex exec --json' prints nothing for one (a turn made to compact five times showed only its items), but the thread's log gets a 'compacted' line each time, with the size of the context it replaced. agent_client.py now reads the log as the turn goes (what was appended since the turn began, at each event and at the end) and prints Claude Code's compact_boundary for each, so a moonshot's compaction with no commit is put to its watcher under either client. The translation of a guessed stream event is gone, the stand-in compacts as Codex does, and the trace's boundary carries the size too. The loop's FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT is not passed to Codex: it is a size for Claude Code's window, and Codex keeps the model's own threshold.

The allow list and the reviewed findings: Codex's sandbox cannot keep them from a patch in a way the tools survive. A file marked 'read' in a permission profile was patched all the same (the automatic reviewer let the request through, as it did for the built-in read-only profile), and one marked 'deny' could not be read by any command, the repository's own tool included, with no way to ask. So the bar is in the tool, for every client: the three commands a person runs (approve and add of the allow list, accept of a review) record each decision they wrote on the machine (person-decisions.json in the state folder, a digest and never the value), and check reports as an error a decision in either file that is neither in the file as published (the newest immutable ancestors of @, asked only when the files change) nor in that record. A person who did take one says so with a new command, vouch, of the allow list, which agents are refused (the tool's own check, a deny rule in .claude/settings.json, a forbidden rule for Codex). The record is a file an agent could write: it catches a mistake or a habit, not a forgery. On this checkout every approved entry is published, so the check finds nothing.

Verified by five new tests (a compaction read from a log once and only if it is the turn's; an approval a person made against one written by hand; a published decision and the cached answer; vouching; an accepted finding) and the changed ones (the adapter through the stand-in over three turns); test_review.py now keeps its state in a folder of its own, since a person's command writes the record. The tests of what changed pass, 23 of 23 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap). The default test run on the merge before this commit passed, 58 of 58 (recorded for tree 93f833f7a9f1).

### A failed turn or compaction ends a loop needing attention, and a single agent's run is checked at its start, its restart and its landing

[`d40391c6811f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/d40391c6811f39ab6ca9759d23bf0859f5ad8a8f) · [log `64bc1004e98b`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/64bc1004e98b7404245a0b2257d225356a31be6448954a35d02f566cb570abdd.jsonl.gz)

An outside review of the Codex work found four things; this takes up what bears on a single agent's run, with the user's decisions of 2026-11-19 (the rule for failed turns holds for every loop; the network is open to Codex workers; list prices for the two Codex models).

A turn that did not end well is not a cycle. feature-loop.sh only logged a worker turn the client had ended with an error (a quota, an interruption) or cut off, and on the last cycle of a count it then skipped the watcher's verdict, compacted, summarized and exited 0; a failed compaction was logged and ignored. It now reads the turn's own event stream: no result, or a result that is not a success, stops the loop with status 1 and a record line that says the session needs attention, before any compaction or summary; a compaction that fails stops it too, after the summary when the run was ending anyway. A turn that ends well with no commit is judged as before. Claude Code's own compaction shows as a boundary in its stream (seen in the logs of earlier runs), which the rule takes for success.

A single run's start and restart. A Codex run now gets the check a brief's Codex streams get, in the agent's folder: the client is there and is given the checkout's CLAUDE.md whole. A restart keeps the count of cycles and the queue's setting of the leg before unless given its own (--cycles N, 0 for none; --verification) and prints what it kept; before, a bare restart dropped the count and turned the queue back on. A restart of a Codex run whose record names a thread, and whose binding is gone, is refused: a new thread would be told to go on with work it never saw.

Decisions only a person takes. One that no person is recorded as having taken now waives nothing (the redactor is given only published or recorded decisions, so the finding stays raised), a new question of sync.py (decisions, with --at REV for a commit) says which there are, and landing a workspace's line asks it first and leaves the line where it is. A push already refuses while check has the error. The user's own approval of b24f7c44, made in their terminal while this was written, left its record and the check finds nothing: the legitimate path works.

Also: the network is open inside a Codex worker's sandbox (probed: a host is not resolved without the setting, reached with it); AGENT_CLIENT_CODEX_SETTINGS gives a rehearsal extra client settings; OpenAI's list prices for gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol are in pricing.json (from developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing, 2026-11-19), with the rates of a prompt over 272K tokens, which metrics.py applies per call; the Stop hook of .codex/hooks.json shows a message while it runs.

Verified by eight new tests and the changed ones: through single_run.py with a one-cycle cap and the Codex stand-in, a turn that fails, one that is cut off, a compaction that fails and a quiet turn that ends well; a restart's kept limits; the instruction check and the lost thread; an unrecorded decision that waives nothing and a line that is asked; landing refused and then allowed; the long-context price. The tests of what changed pass, 26 of 26 Python test files (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run --changed --rust-jobs 1 under an 8G cap).

### Requests to the web are plain, few and one at a time, and a bot check or a refusal means another source

[`bccdbea32d03`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/bccdbea32d039f55206d062a647b47bbc658030e) · [log `29e2f2d886b7`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/e61d882b-5ef7-428e-90df-ffe709ac6962/29e2f2d886b716edcbb8a114051453edec5c03c2fc2fda72558af242b8b61322.jsonl.gz)

Every request an agent sends leaves from the user's own address, and the user decided on 2026-11-19 that agents read the web only in plain, targeted requests at a low volume, so that no site takes the address for a scraper. A new section of the operating notes says so for every tool (curl, scripts, WebFetch, the headless browser): the tool's own User-Agent and no header naming the user or project; a bot check, CAPTCHA, 403, 451 or login wall ends the attempt at that host, with the content read elsewhere or reported unread (one retry of a 429 or 503 after Retry-After); one request at a time, a second apart per host, slower where an API publishes a limit (arXiv 3 s, NVD 6 s); a few dozen requests at most for a task, no crawling, bulk downloads or mirroring; a run's streams share the address; link checks follow the same rules. The research router points at the rule and no longer sends the browser at DBLP's bot check or ACM's 403: DBLP searches go to Crossref or Semantic Scholar, ACM papers to Crossref's metadata and the arXiv or author's copy. The rule's reason names the link check earlier this session that sent 12 requests at a time with a browser-like User-Agent. Verified: test_agent_client.py (24) under a 4G cap; agent_client.py instructions --client codex reports no problems.

### 1. 2026-11-17 12:44 UTC

> Explore `/run-brief` and describe all options that can be passed when invoking a run to me

**Reply:**

`/run-brief` takes four arguments. Its signature, from `.claude/skills/run-brief/SKILL.md`:

```
/run-brief [--no-foundation] [--unattended] [--summary-interval SECONDS] <NAME | llm-dlc/loops/NAME.md>
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **`<brief>`** (required) | The one brief to run, given by name (`domain-advances`) or by file (`llm-dlc/loops/domain-advances.md`). If the request doesn't clearly name one brief, the watcher asks before starting anything. A brief whose status is already `done` isn't run. |
| **`--no-foundation`** | Skips stage 2, the Fable 5.2 session that builds the shared groundwork and updates the plan before the streams start. Stage 2 is also skipped without this flag if a foundation has already landed or a stream's workspace already exists, because that means an earlier run is being continued. |
| **`--unattended`** | Tells the watcher you're away for the whole run. It doesn't bring you anything it can decide and record itself. A question only you can answer is recorded as an open decision (`decisions.py record`, state `open`), and the rest of the run carries on around it. This also covers test failures after a merge, or a foundation that changed what the brief is for: these become open decisions instead of stopping the run. |

The da-* windows show the cost: preservation, challenge and state each stopped to diagnose the failure and rerun the test with the variable unset.

**The fix:** I added `.claude/settings.local.json` to each stream workspace (state, evidence, preservation, challenge). It sets `RUN_STREAMS_WATCHER` to empty for that workspace's Claude sessions.
- **Nothing running is touched.** `run-streams.sh` keeps its own copy of the variable, so merge and blocked questions from the real streams still reach the watcher. Only the sessions it starts lose it, and nothing they run needs it.
- **Takes effect at each stream's next turn.** The loop starts a fresh `claude -p` for every turn, and that process reads the file. Turns already in progress keep the old value until they end.

**What made the test failure a subtle mistake:**
- The checker asks "can I run this call?" in two places: a scan that only sees the bytecode, and the engine, which sees the argument values. Both read one shared list of modelled calls.
- The agent added `String.valueOf(Object)` to that list. That made the scan claim the call is handled for every argument, when the engine only handles a string or null.
- It was following the entry next to it: `Pattern.compile` is already on the list, though it is also only modelled for some arguments.
- An existing test about 2,000 lines away holds the stricter rule. That test, not the model, caught the unsound change.

### 9. 2026-11-17 18:13 UTC

> Summarize I010 for me in the context of the running preservation stream

**Reply:**

## I010: a soundness hole in preservation's relational mechanism

**In one line:** the code the checker treats as "the same in both versions" can miss code that is actually different. When it does, it can prove two versions agree when a JVM shows they don't.

### The mechanism it breaks

Preservation's central result, the ties in commit `owrsowqm` (`lib/src/bmc/ties.rs`), works like this. When both versions run a loop the checker can't unroll fully, the checker summarizes it. If the two sides start the loop with the same **key**, they get one shared set of values rather than independent ones. That shared set is what removed 287's spurious counterexample. The key has three parts:
1. the code: a fingerprint of the method and everything it reaches;
2. the static fields of the classes that code uses;
3. the reachable objects, by class.

All three come from one function, `reach` in `lib/src/shared.rs`. **It skips every call whose owner is a JDK class**, on the reasoning that "the JDK is the same in both versions". That's true of the JDK's own code, but a call through a JDK interface (`IntUnaryOperator`, `Runnable`, `Comparator`, `Object.toString`) can run *application* code. That code is then in no fingerprint, its private helpers are in no class comparison, and the static fields it reads are in no key.

> Would it help for the external expert to scope out / evaluate 307 more deeply prior to agents starting? I am concerned that there is a lot of complexity here and we may take the wrong path.

**Reply:**

Yes, I'd do it, but narrowly: settle the three or four decisions where 307 can go wrong, before preservation reaches step 6. Don't ask the expert for a full design. The timing works: preservation still has the 289/290 rerun (I011) and 287's new wall at `BCrypt.key` ahead of it, so it's likely hours from starting 307.

### Why 307 deserves a look first

307 looks like "the same technique, a second time", but its shape is different from 287 in ways that matter:

1. **The change sits exactly where the checker is weakest.**
   - The old version calls `password.getBytes("UTF-8")` inside a `try` that turns `UnsupportedEncodingException` into `AssertionError`. The new one calls `getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`.
   - The checker models only the second form (`lib/src/bmc/bytes.rs`), so 307's first stop will be at the old version's conversion.
   - Showing the two agree on every UTF-16 string (lone surrogates become `?`, a NUL counts, a null password throws `NullPointerException`) needs facts about the JDK. "UTF-8" is always supported, and both forms replace bad input the same way.
   - Modelling those facts loosely would produce a false proof in exactly the place the claim is about. That's the real soundness risk.

2. **There's a fork in the approach, and the brief points down the costlier branch.**
   - Step 6 says "by the same technique": run both versions' bcrypt, related by the ties.

### 13. 2026-11-17 19:04 UTC

> I'll check with the watcher on that. Does our current framework support companion claims? Any examples?

**Reply:**

Yes, in two senses. The second is the one that matters here.

### 1. Companion examples: a link only

`target.json` has `identity.companions` for related examples, such as a CVE's negative example and its positive one. 307 and 287 name each other this way, as do 305↔285 and 306↔286, and a unit test (`CompanionTest` in `examples/tools/targets/test_packets.py`) checks that each pair names the other. Nothing else uses the link: no evidence or verdict passes between companions.

### 2. Companion claims inside one example: the `parent` field

A task can name a `parent` task. The schema (`examples/schema/target.schema.json`) describes it as "a narrower diagnostic or derived claim: the task it is derived from, which stays unresolved." The rules are spelled out in `examples/tools/targets/workflow_handoff.py`:
- A frozen claim stays as it is. "A semantically changed proposal is a new claim with a parent link, for review."
- "A narrower kernel or a surrogate is a separate task with its own claim and explicit correspondence work; it never discharges this task's obligation without a checked connection."
- A gap closes only when the parent's *unchanged* claim is rerun and decided.

**The one example in use is 287's guard lemma:**
- **Parent** (`vulnerable-security` / `fixed-security`, `claims/overlong-candidate-rejected.json`): the public claim about `BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches` on a candidate String.

## What happened

- **Claude-to-Claude messaging worked earlier because `SendMessage` is a sanctioned channel.** Codex isn't a Claude session, so `SendMessage` can't reach it.
- **It's fragile even when allowed.** Pasted multi-line text can garble, the paste can land while Codex is busy or you're typing in that window, and screen-scraping truncates. There's also no structured reply.

I'd **not** add an allow rule for `tmux send-keys` into agent windows. It removes a safeguard to keep a fragile channel. And having another session do it for you would get round your permission setting, which shouldn't happen either.

### 53. 2026-11-19 15:56 UTC

> What did you just write in the last action?

**Reply:**

I wrote no files. My last action was the progress report; before it I only ran read-only commands like `date`, `grep`, `pipeline.py status` and `report`, and reading the worker's commits and diffs.

**There's one exception I should have avoided.** Running `jj log` and `jj diff` inside the worker's workspace makes jj **snapshot that workspace's working copy**, which is a write to the repository's operation log. The op log shows two snapshots caused by my reviews:

| Time | My command | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 15:37:39 | `jj log -r 'mwmkmrmr::@' …` | recorded the worker's edits so far into its uncommitted change |
| 15:54:59 | the same, in this last check | the same |

My other `jj` commands found nothing new to record, so they left no operation.

**Impact:** harmless this time. A snapshot only records the files already on disk into the worker's uncommitted change, which its own next `jj` command does anyway, and nothing went stale or conflicted. But it isn't strictly read-only. If it had landed at the same moment as one of the worker's jj operations, it could have left a stale working copy for the worker to clean up.

**For later reviews**, I'll add `--ignore-working-copy` to every `jj` command in another session's workspace, which reads without snapshotting. I used it for the op-log check just now. Going further, I'll read the worker's uncommitted state only from its own log (`loop.log`) and the files on disk.
